topics.name: Position, Path Length, and Displacement
topics.summary: Position specifies where an object is on a straight line, measured from a chosen origin with a chosen positive direction — it can be positive, negative, or zero. Path length (distance) is the total length of the actual path travelled, always a non-negative number that only ever increases as the object moves. Displacement is the straight-line change in position, \( \Delta x = x_{\text{final}}-x_{\text{initial}} \), a signed quantity that depends only on the start and end points, never on the path taken between them. The single most important relationship in this topic is that the magnitude of displacement can never exceed the distance travelled, \( |\Delta x|\le\text{distance} \), with equality holding only when the object moves in one direction without ever reversing. Whenever an object doubles back — even partially — distance keeps accumulating while displacement can shrink, stay the same, or even become zero, as in any round trip. Multi-leg journeys are handled by summing each leg's magnitude for distance, and summing each leg's SIGNED value for displacement.
key_formulas: \( |\Delta x| \le \text{distance} \), with equality only when there is no reversal
topics.worked_example: A hiker walks \( 8 \) km east, then \( 3 \) km west. Distance travelled \( = 8+3 = 11 \) km (both legs' magnitudes are added). Displacement \( = 8-3 = 5 \) km east (the westward leg is subtracted, since it's opposite in sign to the first leg). Notice \( |5|<11 \): the reversal on the second leg makes the distance strictly greater than the magnitude of the displacement.
common_mistakes: Reporting distance and displacement as if they were always numerically equal, ignoring any reversal in direction.
Summing the magnitudes of every leg for displacement too, instead of keeping the sign of each leg before adding.
Swapping the two quantities — reporting the signed net change where the unsigned total path length was asked for, or vice versa.
Assuming a return to the starting point means the distance travelled was also zero, rather than just the displacement.

topics.name: Velocity: Average, Instantaneous, and Relative Velocity
topics.summary: Average velocity is the net displacement divided by the total time elapsed, \( \bar{v}=\dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} \) — a signed quantity depending only on the start and end positions. Average speed is the total distance travelled divided by the total time, always non-negative, and it equals the average velocity's magnitude only when there is no reversal in direction. Instantaneous velocity is the derivative of position with respect to time, \( v=\dfrac{dx}{dt} \), found by differentiating a given position function and evaluating it at the instant of interest. A frequent trap is computing average speed for two legs by naively averaging the two given speeds, \( \frac{v_1+v_2}{2} \) — this is only valid when the two legs take EQUAL TIME; when they cover equal DISTANCE instead, the correct combination is the distance-weighted (harmonic-mean-style) formula. Relative velocity between two objects on the same line is found by vector (signed) subtraction of their velocities — added when moving toward each other, subtracted when moving the same way.
key_formulas: \( \bar{v} = \dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} \) (average velocity); \( \text{average speed} = \dfrac{\text{total distance}}{\text{total time}} \)
\( v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} \) (instantaneous velocity, from a position function)
For two equal-distance legs at speeds \( v_1,v_2 \): average speed \( = \dfrac{2v_1v_2}{v_1+v_2} \) (NOT the simple average)
Relative velocity \( = v_1-v_2 \) (signed subtraction, along the common line)
topics.worked_example: A car covers the first half of a journey's DISTANCE at \( 40 \) km/h and the second half at \( 60 \) km/h. The naive average, \( \frac{40+60}{2}=50 \) km/h, is WRONG here because the two halves take different times. The correct average speed is \( \dfrac{2(40)(60)}{40+60}=48 \) km/h — the harmonic mean, since the split is by equal distance, not equal time.
common_mistakes: Using the simple average \( \frac{v_1+v_2}{2} \) for two equal-DISTANCE legs, when it is only valid for two equal-TIME legs.
Treating average speed and average velocity as always numerically equal, ignoring any reversal in direction.
Confusing an instantaneous velocity (evaluated at one instant via differentiation) with an average velocity (computed over an interval).
Adding two objects' velocities when they move in the same direction, or subtracting when they move toward each other — the sign convention must be applied consistently.

topics.name: Acceleration: Average and Instantaneous
topics.summary: Average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time taken, \( \bar{a}=\dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} \), a signed quantity found from just the initial and final velocities regardless of what happened in between. Instantaneous acceleration is the derivative of velocity with respect to time, \( a=\dfrac{dv}{dt} \) (equivalently the second derivative of position), evaluated at a specific instant. A key conceptual subtlety is that velocity and acceleration are independent in sign: an object can have zero velocity while its acceleration is nonzero (a momentary turning point), or nonzero velocity while its acceleration is zero (moving at constant velocity). Whether an object is speeding up or slowing down depends on whether velocity and acceleration share the SAME sign (speeding up) or OPPOSITE signs (slowing down) — not on the sign of acceleration alone. For constant acceleration specifically, the instantaneous and average acceleration are equal at every instant, since averaging a constant quantity simply returns that same constant.
key_formulas: Speeding up when \( v \) and \( a \) share the same sign; slowing down when they have opposite signs
topics.worked_example: A particle has velocity \( v(t)=t^2-6t+5 \) m/s. At \( t=2 \) s: \( v(2)=4-12+5=-3 \) m/s and \( a(2)=2t-6=2(2)-6=-2 \) m/s\(^2\). Since both \( v(2) \) and \( a(2) \) are negative (same sign), the particle is speeding up at this instant, even though its acceleration is negative.
common_mistakes: Assuming zero velocity at an instant automatically means zero acceleration at that same instant, or vice versa.
Concluding an object is slowing down purely because its acceleration is negative, without checking whether the velocity is also negative at that instant.
Computing average acceleration by averaging two SEGMENTS' own accelerations instead of using the overall change in velocity divided by the overall time.
Forgetting that for uniform (constant) acceleration, the instantaneous and average acceleration are the same value at every point in time, not just at one special instant.

topics.name: Kinematic Equations for Uniformly Accelerated Motion
topics.summary: For motion with constant (uniform) acceleration, three standard equations connect initial velocity \( u \), final velocity \( v \), acceleration \( a \), time \( t \), and displacement \( s \): \( v=u+at \), \( s=ut+\tfrac12at^2 \), and \( v^2=u^2+2as \). Each lets you solve for an unknown quantity given the other three, and choosing the right equation depends on which three quantities are already known. The single most important discipline is sign-convention consistency: pick ONE positive direction at the start of a problem (e.g. upward, or the direction of initial motion) and hold every variable — \( u \), \( v \), \( a \), and \( s \) — to that same convention throughout. This is especially critical for vertical motion under gravity: if upward is taken as positive, \( g \) must be entered as NEGATIVE (since gravity acts downward), producing negative accelerations for rises and requiring care with signs on the way down. These equations apply strictly to constant acceleration; they cannot be used directly if the acceleration itself changes with time.
topics.worked_example: A ball is thrown upward with \( u=20 \) m/s (upward positive, \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\), so \( a=-10 \) m/s\(^2\)). Time to reach the highest point (\( v=0 \)): from \( v=u+at \), \( 0=20-10t \), so \( t=2 \) s. Maximum height: from \( v^2=u^2+2as \), \( 0=400-20s \), so \( s=20 \) m.
common_mistakes: Keeping \( g \) positive for a decelerating (upward-thrown) motion when upward has been chosen as the positive direction, instead of correctly taking \( a=-g \).
Mixing sign conventions mid-problem — flipping the sign of only one variable (say, \( a \)) while leaving \( u \), \( v \), or \( s \) in the original convention.
Forgetting the factor of \( \tfrac12 \) in \( s=ut+\tfrac12at^2 \), or the factor of \( 2 \) in \( v^2=u^2+2as \).
Applying these equations to a scenario where the acceleration itself is changing with time, where they no longer hold directly.
When an equation yields two roots (e.g. solving a quadratic in \( t \)), keeping the physically meaningless root (such as a trivial \( t=0 \) or a negative time) instead of the meaningful one.

topics.name: Graphical Analysis of Motion: Position-Time, Velocity-Time, and Acceleration-Time Graphs
topics.summary: Position-time and velocity-time graphs encode motion visually, and reading them correctly comes down to knowing what slope and area represent on each. On a position-time (\( x \)-\( t \)) graph, the SLOPE at any point gives the instantaneous velocity there; a steeper line means a larger speed, a horizontal line means the object is at rest, and a straight line throughout means constant velocity. On a velocity-time (\( v \)-\( t \)) graph, the SLOPE gives the instantaneous acceleration, while the (signed) AREA between the graph and the time-axis over an interval gives the displacement — areas below the axis count as negative, subtracting from areas above it. If total DISTANCE is wanted instead of displacement, every region's area must be taken as a positive magnitude before adding, regardless of which side of the axis it falls on. A common confusion is swapping what slope and area represent between the two graph types, or reading an area's magnitude when the question specifically asks for a signed displacement (or vice versa).
key_formulas: On an \( x \)-\( t \) graph: slope \( = v \) (instantaneous velocity)
On a \( v \)-\( t \) graph: slope \( = a \) (instantaneous acceleration)
On a \( v \)-\( t \) graph: signed area under the curve \( = \) displacement; sum of area MAGNITUDES \( = \) distance
topics.worked_example: A \( v \)-\( t \) graph shows \( +10 \) m/s from \( t=0 \) s to \( t=3 \) s, then \( -4 \) m/s from \( t=3 \) s to \( t=5 \) s. Displacement (signed areas added): \( 10(3)+(-4)(2)=30-8=22 \) m. Distance (magnitudes added): \( |30|+|-8|=38 \) m — larger than the displacement, because of the direction reversal at \( t=3 \) s.
common_mistakes: Reading the slope of a \( v \)-\( t \) graph as velocity instead of acceleration, or the slope of an \( x \)-\( t \) graph as acceleration instead of velocity.
Computing the area under a \( v \)-\( t \) graph as distance when displacement was actually asked for, ignoring that regions below the time-axis should subtract rather than add.
Reading only a graph's endpoint value as if it were the object's average velocity, instead of correctly computing the slope or area.
Assuming a graph's slope or area over one sub-interval applies to the whole duration shown, instead of using only the relevant portion of the graph.

questions.topic: Position, Path Length, and Displacement
questions.question: A car travels from point A to point B along a straight road and then returns to point A along the same road. Which of the following is necessarily true about this trip?
options: The displacement is zero, and the distance travelled is twice the length of the road AB.
The distance travelled is zero, and the displacement is twice the length of the road AB.
Both the displacement and the distance travelled are zero.
Both the displacement and the distance travelled equal the length of the road AB.
questions.explanation:
Displacement depends only on the initial and final position. Since the car returns to A, the initial and final positions coincide, so the displacement is \( 0 \).

Distance, however, is the total path length covered, which includes both the outward and return legs, so it equals \( 2 \times AB \).
questions.hint: Ask separately: did the position change overall (displacement), and how much ground was actually covered (distance)?
distractor_logic: Swaps the two quantities — confuses which one measures the total path covered (distance) and which one measures the net change in position (displacement).
Incorrectly assumes distance also cancels on the return trip, when only displacement (a signed quantity) can go to zero this way.
Ignores the return leg entirely, as if the car stopped at B instead of coming back to A.

questions.topic: Position, Path Length, and Displacement
questions.question: An object moves along a straight line from position \( x = 2 \) m to position \( x = 9 \) m without changing direction. What is its displacement?
questions.explanation:
Displacement is the change in position: \( \Delta x = x_{f} - x_{i} \).

Here \( \Delta x = 9 - 2 = 7 \) m, and since \( x \) increased, the direction is positive.
questions.hint: Subtract the initial position from the final position — don't just read off the final coordinate.
distractor_logic: Uses only the final position value, forgetting to subtract the starting position.
Adds the initial and final positions instead of subtracting them.
Gets the correct magnitude but assigns the wrong sign/direction to the displacement.

questions.topic: Position, Path Length, and Displacement
questions.question: A student walks \( 6 \) m to the east and then walks back \( 6 \) m to the west, returning to the starting point. What are the total distance travelled and the magnitude of the displacement?
questions.explanation:
Distance adds up every metre actually walked: \( 6 + 6 = 12 \) m.

Displacement depends only on start and end position; since the student returns to the starting point, displacement \( = 0 \) m.
questions.hint: The walk ends where it started — what does that tell you about the net change in position?
distractor_logic: Swaps the distance and displacement values with each other.
Treats the return leg as if it added to the net position change instead of cancelling the outward leg.
Counts only one leg of the walk instead of the full path covered in both directions.

questions.topic: Position, Path Length, and Displacement
questions.question: The position of a particle on a straight line changes from \( x_1 = -3 \) m to \( x_2 = 5 \) m. What is its displacement?
questions.explanation:
Displacement \( = x_2 - x_1 = 5 - (-3) = 8 \) m.

Since \( x_2 > x_1 \), the direction is positive.
questions.hint: Be careful with the negative sign of \( x_1 \) when subtracting.
distractor_logic: Adds the two signed positions \( (5 + (-3) = 2) \) instead of subtracting them.
Gets the correct magnitude but assigns the wrong (negative) direction.
Uses only the magnitude of the initial position, ignoring the final position entirely.

questions.topic: Position, Path Length, and Displacement
questions.question: A cyclist rides \( 4 \) km due north and then continues another \( 3 \) km due north without stopping or reversing. What are the total distance travelled and the magnitude of the displacement?
questions.explanation:
Since the cyclist never reverses direction, every metre of distance also counts toward displacement.

Distance \( = 4 + 3 = 7 \) km, and displacement (same direction throughout) is also \( 7 \) km.
questions.hint: With no reversal in direction, how do distance and displacement compare?
distractor_logic: Subtracts the two legs as if the second leg partly reversed the first, even though both legs are northward.
Swaps a wrongly computed displacement with the correctly computed distance.
Multiplies the two legs instead of adding them, giving a displacement larger than the distance, which is impossible.

questions.topic: Position, Path Length, and Displacement
questions.question: A jogger runs \( 8 \) m to the east and then \( 5 \) m to the west. What are the total distance travelled and the magnitude of the displacement?
questions.explanation:
Distance sums the magnitudes of both legs regardless of direction: \( 8 + 5 = 13 \) m.

Displacement is the net change: \( 8 \) m east minus \( 5 \) m west \( = 3 \) m east, so its magnitude is \( 3 \) m.
questions.hint: Distance never cares about direction; displacement is the net effect of both legs.
distractor_logic: Swaps the distance and displacement values with each other.
Treats both legs as if they were in the same direction, ignoring that the second leg partly cancels the first.
Subtracts the two legs to get distance instead of adding their magnitudes, undercounting the path actually covered.

questions.topic: Position, Path Length, and Displacement
questions.question: Which of the following statements about distance and displacement is always true for motion along a straight line?
options: The distance travelled can never exceed the magnitude of displacement.
Distance and displacement are always numerically equal.
The magnitude of displacement can never exceed the distance travelled.
Displacement is always positive, while distance can be negative.
questions.explanation:
Displacement measures only the net change in position, while distance measures the entire path covered.

Since any reversal in direction adds to distance without adding to (and sometimes reducing) net displacement, the magnitude of displacement can never exceed the distance travelled.
questions.hint: Think of a round trip: distance is large, but displacement can shrink all the way to zero.
distractor_logic: Reverses the correct inequality between the two quantities.
Ignores that distance and displacement are equal only when the motion never reverses direction — otherwise distance is strictly larger.
Incorrectly assigns sign behaviour: distance (a path length) is never negative, while displacement can be negative, not the other way around.

questions.topic: Position, Path Length, and Displacement
questions.question: A parked car remains at the same position \( x = 4 \) m on a straight road for \( 10 \) minutes. What are the distance travelled and the displacement during this interval?
questions.explanation:
Since the car never moves, its position at the end of the interval is the same as at the start.

Both distance travelled and displacement depend on motion having occurred, so both are \( 0 \) m; the coordinate \( x = 4 \) m is just where the car happens to be parked, not a measure of motion.
questions.hint: The car's fixed coordinate is not the same thing as how far it moved.
distractor_logic: Mistakes the car's fixed coordinate for a nonzero displacement, even though position never changes over the interval.
Mistakes the car's fixed coordinate for a nonzero distance travelled, even though the car never moves.
Uses the coordinate value \( x = 4 \) m for both quantities instead of recognising that no motion occurred at all.

questions.topic: Velocity: Average, Instantaneous, and Relative Velocity
questions.question: A car travels \( 150 \) km in \( 3 \) hours along a straight highway without reversing direction. What is its average velocity?
questions.explanation: Average velocity \( = \dfrac{\text{displacement}}{\text{time}} = \dfrac{150}{3} = 50 \) km/h, in the direction of travel.
questions.hint: Divide the total displacement by the total time taken.
distractor_logic: Multiplies distance and time together instead of dividing.
Inverts the ratio, computing time divided by distance instead of distance divided by time.
Treats the time value alone as the answer, ignoring the distance altogether.

questions.topic: Velocity: Average, Instantaneous, and Relative Velocity
questions.question: A particle's position changes from \( x = -4 \) m to \( x = 16 \) m in a time interval of \( 5 \) s. What is its average velocity?
questions.explanation: Displacement \( = 16-(-4) = 20 \) m. Average velocity \( = \dfrac{20}{5} = 4 \) m/s, in the positive \( x \)-direction.
questions.hint: Find the displacement first, then divide by the time interval.
distractor_logic: Computes the displacement correctly but forgets to divide by the time interval.
Adds the initial and final positions \( (-4+16=12) \) instead of subtracting them to find the displacement.
Gets the correct magnitude but assigns the wrong direction to the average velocity.

questions.topic: Velocity: Average, Instantaneous, and Relative Velocity
questions.question: A cyclist completes a round trip, riding \( 10 \) km to a park and then \( 10 \) km back home along the same road, taking \( 2 \) hours in total. What are her average speed and average velocity for the entire trip?
options: Average speed \( = 0 \) km/h, average velocity \( = 10 \) km/h
Both average speed and average velocity are \( 10 \) km/h
Average speed \( = 10 \) km/h, average velocity \( = 0 \) km/h
Both average speed and average velocity are \( 0 \) km/h
questions.explanation:
Average speed \( = \dfrac{\text{total distance}}{\text{time}} = \dfrac{20}{2} = 10 \) km/h.

Average velocity \( = \dfrac{\text{displacement}}{\text{time}} = \dfrac{0}{2} = 0 \) km/h, since she returns to her starting point.
questions.hint: The round trip gives zero net displacement, but the wheels still covered real distance both ways.
distractor_logic: Swaps the average speed and average velocity values with each other.
Assumes average speed and average velocity are always numerically equal, ignoring that this trip involves a reversal in direction.
Wrongly assumes that because the displacement is zero, the total distance travelled must also be zero.

questions.topic: Velocity: Average, Instantaneous, and Relative Velocity
questions.question: Car A travels at \( 60 \) km/h and Car B travels at \( 40 \) km/h, both moving in the same direction along a straight highway. What is the velocity of Car A relative to Car B?
options: \( 100 \) km/h, in the direction both cars are moving
\( 20 \) km/h, opposite to the direction both cars are moving
\( 40 \) km/h, in the direction both cars are moving
\( 20 \) km/h, in the direction both cars are moving
questions.explanation: For two objects moving in the same direction, the relative velocity is the difference of their velocities: \( 60-40=20 \) km/h, in the direction of motion.
questions.hint: Same direction means subtract; opposite directions would mean add.
distractor_logic: Adds the two speeds instead of subtracting them, which is only correct when the two objects move in opposite directions.
Gets the correct magnitude but assigns the wrong direction to the relative velocity.
Reports one car's own speed instead of computing the relative velocity between the two cars.

questions.topic: Velocity: Average, Instantaneous, and Relative Velocity
questions.question: Train P moves at \( 70 \) km/h to the east and Train Q moves at \( 50 \) km/h to the west, along parallel straight tracks. What is the velocity of Train P relative to Train Q?
questions.explanation:
Taking east as positive: \( v_P = 70 \) km/h, \( v_Q = -50 \) km/h.

Relative velocity of P with respect to Q \( = v_P - v_Q = 70-(-50) = 120 \) km/h, towards the east.
questions.hint: For objects moving in opposite directions, their relative velocity adds the two speeds together.
distractor_logic: Subtracts the two speeds as if both trains moved in the same direction, instead of adding them for trains approaching from opposite directions.
Gets the correct magnitude but assigns the wrong direction to the relative velocity.
Reports one train's own speed instead of computing the relative velocity between the two trains.

questions.topic: Velocity: Average, Instantaneous, and Relative Velocity
questions.question: For any journey along a straight line, which relationship between average speed and the magnitude of average velocity is always true?
options: Average speed is always less than the magnitude of average velocity.
Average speed is always greater than or equal to the magnitude of average velocity.
Average speed and the magnitude of average velocity are always exactly equal.
There is no general relationship between the two; either could be larger.
questions.explanation:
Average speed \( = \dfrac{\text{total distance}}{\text{time}} \) and average velocity's magnitude \( = \dfrac{|\text{displacement}|}{\text{time}} \).

Since distance is always greater than or equal to the magnitude of displacement, average speed is always greater than or equal to the magnitude of average velocity.
questions.hint: This follows directly from the fact that distance can never be smaller than the magnitude of displacement.
distractor_logic: Reverses the correct inequality between average speed and the magnitude of average velocity.
Ignores that they are equal only in the special case of motion without any reversal in direction.
Misses that distance being always at least as large as the magnitude of displacement fixes a one-way relationship, not an arbitrary one.

questions.topic: Velocity: Average, Instantaneous, and Relative Velocity
questions.question: A car's speedometer reads \( 45 \) km/h at a certain moment while travelling along a straight highway. This reading corresponds to which physical quantity?
options: The car's average velocity over the entire trip.
The total distance the car has travelled so far.
The magnitude of the car's instantaneous velocity at that moment.
The car's average speed since the trip began.
questions.explanation: A speedometer reading is a snapshot at one instant, so it represents the magnitude of the instantaneous velocity at that moment, not any quantity computed over an interval.
questions.hint: Ask whether the reading depends on the whole trip's history, or only on this one instant.
distractor_logic: Confuses a reading at one specific instant with a quantity that must be computed over an entire time interval.
Confuses a rate (speed) with a total accumulated quantity (distance), which the speedometer does not display.
Confuses the instantaneous reading with an averaged quantity computed over the whole journey rather than at this single moment.

questions.topic: Velocity: Average, Instantaneous, and Relative Velocity
questions.question: Two cars travel in the same direction along a straight road, each at a constant \( 55 \) km/h. What is the velocity of one car relative to the other?
options: \( 110 \) km/h, in the direction of motion
\( 55 \) km/h, in the direction of motion
\( 0 \) km/h — both cars must actually be at rest.
\( 0 \) km/h — each car appears stationary relative to the other.
questions.explanation: Relative velocity \( = 55 - 55 = 0 \) km/h. Since both cars move at the same velocity, each appears at rest relative to the other, even though both are moving relative to the road.
questions.hint: Subtract the two velocities — equal velocities always give zero relative velocity, regardless of their actual speed.
distractor_logic: Adds the two speeds instead of subtracting them, which would only be appropriate for objects moving in opposite directions.
Reports one car's own speed instead of subtracting to find the relative velocity between the two cars.
Confuses a zero relative velocity (equal speeds, same direction) with the cars actually being at rest with respect to the road.

questions.topic: Acceleration: Average and Instantaneous
questions.question: A car's velocity increases from \( 10 \) m/s to \( 30 \) m/s in \( 5 \) s while moving in a straight line. What is its average acceleration?
questions.explanation: Average acceleration \( = \dfrac{v-u}{t} = \dfrac{30-10}{5} = 4 \) m/s\(^2\).
questions.hint: Divide the change in velocity by the time taken, not by anything else.
distractor_logic: Computes the change in velocity correctly but forgets to divide by the time interval.
Adds the initial and final velocities instead of subtracting them to find the change in velocity.
Inverts the ratio, computing time divided by the change in velocity instead of the other way around.

questions.topic: Acceleration: Average and Instantaneous
questions.question: A train moving at \( 25 \) m/s applies its brakes and comes to rest in \( 10 \) s. What is its average acceleration?
questions.explanation: Average acceleration \( = \dfrac{v-u}{t} = \dfrac{0-25}{10} = -2.5 \) m/s\(^2\); the negative sign shows the train is decelerating.
questions.hint: The train is slowing down, so its acceleration must carry a negative sign (opposite to its direction of motion).
distractor_logic: Gets the correct magnitude but drops the negative sign, even though the train is slowing down.
Inverts the ratio, computing time divided by the change in velocity instead of the other way around.
Reports only the change in velocity with its correct sign but forgets to divide by the time interval.

questions.topic: Acceleration: Average and Instantaneous
questions.question: A particle moving in the positive \( x \)-direction has a negative acceleration. What does this indicate about its motion at this instant?
options: The particle is speeding up while moving in the positive direction.
The particle must already be moving in the negative direction.
The particle is slowing down (decelerating) while still moving in the positive direction.
The particle is necessarily at rest.
questions.explanation: When acceleration is opposite in sign to velocity, it opposes the motion, so a positive velocity with negative acceleration means the particle is slowing down while still moving forward.
questions.hint: Compare the sign of the acceleration to the sign of the velocity — same sign speeds up, opposite sign slows down.
distractor_logic: Assumes speeding up regardless of the relationship between the signs of velocity and acceleration.
Confuses the sign of acceleration with the sign of velocity itself, assuming a negative acceleration means the particle is already moving backward.
Wrongly assumes any nonzero acceleration must mean the particle is momentarily at rest, ignoring its already positive velocity.

questions.topic: Acceleration: Average and Instantaneous
questions.question: A particle moves along a straight line with a constant velocity of \( 15 \) m/s. What is its acceleration?
options: It cannot be determined without knowing the time interval.
questions.explanation: Acceleration measures the rate of change of velocity. Since the velocity is constant (unchanging), its rate of change — and hence the acceleration — is \( 0 \) m/s\(^2\).
questions.hint: A velocity that never changes has, by definition, no rate of change.
distractor_logic: Confuses the constant velocity value itself with the acceleration, mistaking a velocity reading for a rate of change.
Wrongly assumes acceleration always requires additional time data, missing that a constant velocity already implies a zero rate of change.
Invents an unstated time interval to arbitrarily convert the velocity into an acceleration value.

questions.topic: Acceleration: Average and Instantaneous
questions.question: A sprinter starts from rest and reaches a velocity of \( 8 \) m/s after \( 2 \) s. What is her average acceleration?
questions.explanation: Average acceleration \( = \dfrac{v-u}{t} = \dfrac{8-0}{2} = 4 \) m/s\(^2\).
questions.hint: Divide the change in velocity by the time interval; starting from rest means \( u=0 \).
distractor_logic: Multiplies the change in velocity and the time instead of dividing.
Inverts the ratio, computing time divided by the change in velocity instead of the other way around.
Computes the change in velocity correctly but forgets to divide by the time interval.

questions.topic: Acceleration: Average and Instantaneous
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the instantaneous acceleration of a particle at a specific time \( t \)?
options: The change in velocity divided by the total time of the entire journey.
The rate of change of velocity with respect to time, evaluated exactly at that instant, i.e. \( \dfrac{dv}{dt} \) at \( t \).
The change in position divided by the change in time at that instant.
The velocity of the particle at that instant.
questions.explanation: Instantaneous acceleration is the derivative of velocity with respect to time, evaluated at one specific instant — not an average over the whole trip and not the same thing as velocity itself.
questions.hint: Instantaneous acceleration is to velocity what instantaneous velocity is to position.
distractor_logic: Describes average acceleration over the whole journey rather than the instantaneous value at one specific time.
Describes velocity (rate of change of position), not acceleration (rate of change of velocity).
Confuses acceleration with velocity itself, rather than the rate at which velocity is changing.

questions.topic: Acceleration: Average and Instantaneous
questions.question: An object's velocity changes from \( -6 \) m/s to \( -2 \) m/s over \( 4 \) s while moving along a straight line. What is its average acceleration?
questions.explanation: Average acceleration \( = \dfrac{v-u}{t} = \dfrac{-2-(-6)}{4} = \dfrac{4}{4} = 1 \) m/s\(^2\).
questions.hint: Carefully subtract the signed initial velocity from the signed final velocity before dividing by time.
distractor_logic: Gets the correct magnitude but assigns the wrong sign to the acceleration.
Adds the two signed velocities instead of subtracting them to find the change in velocity.
Computes the change in velocity correctly but forgets to divide by the time interval.

questions.topic: Acceleration: Average and Instantaneous
questions.question: What are the SI units of acceleration?
questions.explanation: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity (m/s) with respect to time (s), giving units of \( \text{m/s}\div\text{s} = \text{m/s}^2 \).
questions.hint: Divide the units of velocity by the units of time once more.
distractor_logic: Gives the units of velocity instead of acceleration.
Gives the units of distance or position instead of acceleration.
Inverts the correct units, placing time squared over distance instead of distance over time squared.

questions.topic: Kinematic Equations for Uniformly Accelerated Motion
questions.question: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at \( 2 \) m/s\(^2\) for \( 5 \) s. What is its final velocity?
questions.hint: Starting from rest means \( u=0 \); apply \( v=u+at \) directly.
distractor_logic: Adds \( a \) and \( t \) instead of multiplying them.
Uses only the time value as the final velocity, ignoring the acceleration and initial velocity.
Accidentally computes \( \tfrac12at^2 \) (the displacement formula) instead of \( u+at \).

questions.topic: Kinematic Equations for Uniformly Accelerated Motion
questions.question: An object starts with an initial velocity of \( 4 \) m/s and accelerates uniformly at \( 3 \) m/s\(^2\) for \( 4 \) s. What is its displacement during this time?
questions.hint: Remember the displacement formula has two separate terms — don't drop either one.
distractor_logic: Computes only the \( ut \) term, forgetting the \( \tfrac12at^2 \) contribution entirely.
Computes only the \( \tfrac12at^2 \) term, forgetting the \( ut \) contribution entirely.
Forgets the factor of \( \tfrac12 \) in the second term, computing \( ut+at^2 \) instead.

questions.topic: Kinematic Equations for Uniformly Accelerated Motion
questions.question: A ball is thrown with an initial velocity of \( 6 \) m/s and undergoes a uniform acceleration of \( 4 \) m/s\(^2\) over a displacement of \( 8 \) m. What is its final velocity?
questions.hint: After computing \( v^2 \), remember to take the square root to get \( v \).
distractor_logic: Forgets to take the square root at the end, leaving the answer as \( v^2 \) instead of \( v \).
Uses \( u \) directly instead of \( u^2 \) in the formula, computing \( u+2as \) instead of \( u^2+2as \).
Adds \( u \) and \( \sqrt{2as} \) separately instead of correctly adding \( u^2 \) and \( 2as \) before taking the square root of the sum.

questions.topic: Kinematic Equations for Uniformly Accelerated Motion
questions.question: A cyclist increases her velocity from \( 3 \) m/s to \( 15 \) m/s in \( 6 \) s, uniformly. What is her acceleration?
questions.explanation: Using \( v=u+at \) rearranged: \( a=\dfrac{v-u}{t} = \dfrac{15-3}{6} = 2 \) m/s\(^2\).
questions.hint: Divide the change in velocity by the time taken.
distractor_logic: Computes the change in velocity correctly but forgets to divide by the time interval.
Adds the initial and final velocities instead of subtracting them.
Inverts the ratio, computing time divided by the change in velocity instead of the other way around.

questions.topic: Kinematic Equations for Uniformly Accelerated Motion
questions.question: A train decelerates uniformly from \( 30 \) m/s to \( 10 \) m/s with an acceleration of \( -4 \) m/s\(^2\). How long does this take?
questions.explanation: Using \( v=u+at \) rearranged: \( t=\dfrac{v-u}{a} = \dfrac{10-30}{-4} = \dfrac{-20}{-4} = 5 \) s.
questions.hint: Carefully divide two negative quantities — the result should come out positive, since time cannot be negative.
distractor_logic: Keeps the wrong overall sign by not correctly cancelling the two negative quantities in the division.
Forgets to divide by the acceleration and reports only the magnitude of the velocity change.
Inverts the ratio, dividing the acceleration by the velocity change instead of the other way round.

questions.topic: Kinematic Equations for Uniformly Accelerated Motion
questions.question: A stone, thrown vertically, reaches a velocity of \( 0 \) m/s exactly \( 3 \) s after being thrown, decelerating uniformly under gravity at \( -10 \) m/s\(^2\) (taking upward as positive). What was its initial velocity?
questions.hint: Rearrange \( v=u+at \) to isolate \( u \) before substituting the signed value of \( a \).
distractor_logic: Solves \( u=at \) directly (dropping the true relation \( v=u+at \)) and keeps the negative sign of the acceleration term.
Forgets to multiply the acceleration by the time, using \( u=-a \) instead of \( u=-at \).
Mixes up the equation as \( 0=u+a+t \) and solves \( u=-a-t=10-3=7 \).

questions.topic: Kinematic Equations for Uniformly Accelerated Motion
questions.question: A particle starts with velocity \( 5 \) m/s and has a known constant acceleration and a known time interval, but its displacement is unknown. Which kinematic equation is most directly suited to finding the displacement?
options: \( v=u+at \), since it can be rearranged to give displacement directly
\( v^2=u^2+2as \), since it always applies regardless of which quantities are known
\( s=ut+\tfrac12at^2 \), since it directly relates displacement to the known quantities \( u, a, \) and \( t \)
None of the equations can give displacement without also knowing the final velocity
questions.explanation: \( s=ut+\tfrac12at^2 \) uses exactly the three known quantities \( u \), \( a \), and \( t \) to give displacement directly, without needing the final velocity at all.
questions.hint: Check which equation's variables match exactly what's known and what's being asked for.
distractor_logic: Misidentifies \( v=u+at \), which relates velocity, acceleration, and time but does not involve displacement at all.
Wrongly assumes this equation is the default choice regardless of which quantities are actually known, when it specifically needs displacement or final velocity to be usable here.
Overlooks that \( s=ut+\tfrac12at^2 \) already provides displacement using exactly the three known quantities, without needing the final velocity.

questions.topic: Kinematic Equations for Uniformly Accelerated Motion
questions.question: Before applying the equations \( v=u+at \), \( s=ut+\tfrac12at^2 \), and \( v^2=u^2+2as \) to a problem, what is essential regarding the signs of \( u, v, a, \) and \( s \)?
options: Only the acceleration needs a sign; the other quantities can be treated as positive magnitudes.
Each equation can use its own independent sign convention, chosen separately for convenience.
Signs only matter if the object changes direction during the motion; otherwise they can be ignored.
All four quantities must be assigned signs based on one single, consistently chosen positive direction, used throughout the entire problem.
questions.explanation: A single, fixed sign convention (e.g. \"upward positive\") must be chosen once and applied consistently to \( u, v, a, \) and \( s \) throughout the whole problem — mixing conventions mid-problem gives wrong answers.
questions.hint: Pick one positive direction at the start and stick with it for every quantity in every equation you use.
distractor_logic: Wrongly singles out acceleration as the only quantity needing a sign, when velocity and displacement are equally signed quantities in this convention.
Wrongly allows a different sign convention for each equation, when a single problem must use one fixed convention throughout.
Wrongly assumes sign convention is only relevant during a reversal, when even purely one-directional problems still need a consistent sign assigned to that direction.

questions.topic: Graphical Analysis of Motion: Position-Time, Velocity-Time, and Acceleration-Time Graphs
questions.question: On a position-time (\( x \)-\( t \)) graph for one-dimensional motion, what physical quantity does the slope of the graph at any point represent?
options: The velocity of the object at that instant
The acceleration of the object at that instant
The speed only, never a signed quantity
The total distance travelled up to that instant
questions.explanation: The slope of an \( x \)-\( t \) graph is \( \dfrac{dx}{dt} \), which is precisely the definition of (instantaneous) velocity.
questions.hint: Slope on an \( x \)-\( t \) graph is a rate of change of position — that rate of change is, by definition, velocity.
distractor_logic: Confuses the slope of the \( x \)-\( t \) graph with the slope of a \( v \)-\( t \) graph, which gives acceleration instead.
Wrongly claims the slope can never carry a sign, when in fact a negative slope correctly indicates motion in the negative direction.
Confuses the graph's slope (a rate) with the area under a different graph (an accumulated quantity).

questions.topic: Graphical Analysis of Motion: Position-Time, Velocity-Time, and Acceleration-Time Graphs
questions.question: On a velocity-time (\( v \)-\( t \)) graph, what physical quantity does the slope at any point represent?
options: The velocity of the object at that instant
The acceleration of the object at that instant
The displacement of the object up to that instant
The total distance travelled up to that instant
questions.explanation: The slope of a \( v \)-\( t \) graph is \( \dfrac{dv}{dt} \), which is precisely the definition of (instantaneous) acceleration.
questions.hint: Slope is always a rate of change of whatever is plotted on the vertical axis — here that's velocity, so its rate of change is acceleration.
distractor_logic: Confuses the slope of the \( v \)-\( t \) graph with the quantity plotted on its own vertical axis, which is velocity, not the slope.
Confuses slope (a rate) with area (an accumulated quantity), which is what actually gives displacement on a \( v \)-\( t \) graph.
Confuses slope (a rate) with area (an accumulated quantity), and additionally confuses displacement with total distance.

questions.topic: Graphical Analysis of Motion: Position-Time, Velocity-Time, and Acceleration-Time Graphs
questions.question: On a velocity-time graph, what does the area between the graph and the time-axis over some interval represent (with area below the axis counted as negative)?
options: The total distance travelled over that interval
The average velocity over that interval
The displacement of the object over that interval
questions.explanation: Since velocity is the rate of change of position, the accumulated area under a \( v \)-\( t \) graph (signed, so area below the axis subtracts) gives the net change in position — the displacement.
questions.hint: Area under a \( v \)-\( t \) graph accumulates velocity over time; accumulating a rate over time gives the total change, i.e. displacement, not distance.
distractor_logic: Confuses displacement with total distance, which would instead require taking every region's area as positive (ignoring the sign convention below the axis).
Confuses the accumulated area (displacement) with a single averaged rate (average velocity), which is a different quantity.
Confuses area (an accumulated quantity) with slope (a rate), which is what actually gives acceleration on a \( v \)-\( t \) graph.

questions.topic: Graphical Analysis of Motion: Position-Time, Velocity-Time, and Acceleration-Time Graphs
questions.question: A position-time graph is a straight line passing through \( (0\text{ s}, 0\text{ m}) \) and \( (5\text{ s}, 20\text{ m}) \). What is the velocity of the object?
questions.explanation: Velocity \( = \) slope \( = \dfrac{20-0}{5-0} = 4 \) m/s.
questions.hint: Divide the change in position by the change in time — don't just read off the position value.
distractor_logic: Reads off only the final position value \( 20 \) m, mistaking a coordinate on the graph for the velocity.
Inverts the slope, computing \( \dfrac{5}{20} \) (time over position) instead of \( \dfrac{20}{5} \) (position over time).
Multiplies the position and time values together (\( 20\times5 \)) instead of dividing.

questions.topic: Graphical Analysis of Motion: Position-Time, Velocity-Time, and Acceleration-Time Graphs
questions.question: A velocity-time graph is a straight line from \( (0\text{ s}, 2\text{ m/s}) \) to \( (5\text{ s}, 12\text{ m/s}) \). What is the acceleration of the object?
questions.explanation: Acceleration \( = \) slope \( = \dfrac{12-2}{5-0} = \dfrac{10}{5} = 2 \) m/s\(^2\).
questions.hint: Use the CHANGE in velocity (final minus initial), not the final velocity alone, divided by the time elapsed.
distractor_logic: Divides the final velocity value \( 12 \) directly by the time \( 5 \), instead of first subtracting the initial velocity.
Computes the change in velocity \( (12-2=10) \) correctly but forgets to divide by the time interval.
Inverts the slope, computing \( \dfrac{5}{10} \) (time over velocity change) instead of \( \dfrac{10}{5} \).

questions.topic: Graphical Analysis of Motion: Position-Time, Velocity-Time, and Acceleration-Time Graphs
questions.question: A velocity-time graph shows a constant velocity of \( 10 \) m/s from \( t=0 \) s to \( t=6 \) s. What is the displacement of the object over this interval?
questions.explanation: For constant velocity, the area under the \( v \)-\( t \) graph is a rectangle: displacement \( = 10\times6 = 60 \) m.
questions.hint: The area under a \( v \)-\( t \) graph for constant velocity is simply velocity multiplied by time — a rectangle.
distractor_logic: Reads off only the velocity value, forgetting to multiply by the time duration at all.
Inverts the calculation, dividing time by velocity (\( \dfrac{6}{10} \)) instead of multiplying velocity by time.
Adds the velocity and time values together (\( 10+6 \)) instead of multiplying them.

questions.topic: Graphical Analysis of Motion: Position-Time, Velocity-Time, and Acceleration-Time Graphs
questions.question: A position-time graph is a horizontal straight line (constant \( x \)) over some interval. What does this indicate about the object's motion during that interval?
options: The object is moving with constant nonzero velocity
The object is undergoing constant nonzero acceleration
The object is at rest (its velocity is zero)
The object is at the origin only for a single instant
questions.explanation: A horizontal line on an \( x \)-\( t \) graph has zero slope, and slope on this graph gives velocity — so the velocity is zero throughout, meaning the object is at rest.
questions.hint: Slope of an \( x \)-\( t \) graph gives velocity; what is the slope of a perfectly horizontal line?
distractor_logic: Confuses a horizontal position-time line (zero slope, hence zero velocity) with a horizontal velocity-time line (which would instead indicate constant nonzero velocity).
Wrongly infers a nonzero acceleration from a graph that in fact shows zero velocity throughout, with no change in velocity at all.
Misreads a line that is constant over an entire interval as touching a single value only momentarily.

questions.topic: Graphical Analysis of Motion: Position-Time, Velocity-Time, and Acceleration-Time Graphs
questions.question: A velocity-time graph is a horizontal straight line at a nonzero value over some interval. What does this indicate about the object's motion during that interval?
options: The object is at rest during that interval
The object undergoes constant nonzero acceleration during that interval
The object's position remains constant during that interval
The object moves with constant velocity (zero acceleration) during that interval
questions.explanation: A horizontal line on a \( v \)-\( t \) graph has zero slope, and slope on this graph gives acceleration — so the acceleration is zero while the velocity itself stays fixed at its nonzero value.
questions.hint: Slope of a \( v \)-\( t \) graph gives acceleration; a perfectly horizontal line has zero slope, regardless of the height at which it sits.
distractor_logic: Confuses a horizontal velocity-time line (zero acceleration, nonzero velocity) with a horizontal position-time line (which would instead indicate the object is at rest).
Wrongly infers nonzero acceleration from a graph whose slope is in fact zero throughout.
Confuses the velocity-time graph with a position-time graph, wrongly concluding the object's position stays fixed.

questions.topic: Position, Path Length, and Displacement
questions.question: A particle moves \( 10 \) m in the positive \( x \)-direction, then \( 6 \) m in the negative \( x \)-direction, and finally \( 4 \) m in the positive \( x \)-direction. What are the total distance travelled and the displacement?
options: Distance \( = 20 \) m, displacement \( = 8 \) m in the positive \( x \)-direction
Distance \( = 8 \) m, displacement \( = 20 \) m in the positive \( x \)-direction
Distance \( = 20 \) m, displacement \( = 20 \) m in the positive \( x \)-direction
questions.explanation:
Distance sums every leg's magnitude: \( 10 + 6 + 4 = 20 \) m.

Displacement sums each leg with its sign: \( 10 - 6 + 4 = 8 \) m in the positive \( x \)-direction.
questions.hint: Give the middle leg a negative sign before adding, since it's in the opposite direction.
distractor_logic: Swaps the distance and displacement values with each other.
Adds all three legs as unsigned magnitudes for displacement too, ignoring that the middle leg is a reversal.
Wrongly assumes the particle ends up back at its starting point.

questions.topic: Position, Path Length, and Displacement
questions.question: Starting from the origin, a person walks \( 10 \) m forward, then \( 4 \) m backward, and then \( 2 \) m forward again. What are the total distance travelled and the final displacement from the origin?
questions.explanation:
Distance: \( 10 + 4 + 2 = 16 \) m.

Displacement (signed sum, forward positive): \( 10 - 4 + 2 = 8 \) m forward.
questions.hint: Make sure every one of the three legs is included when you total the net displacement.
distractor_logic: Swaps the distance and displacement values with each other.
Sums all three legs as magnitudes for displacement too, ignoring that the backward leg should be subtracted.
Leaves out the final \( 2 \) m forward leg when computing the net displacement, stopping after only two legs.

questions.topic: Position, Path Length, and Displacement
questions.question: The position of a particle is recorded as \( x(0\text{ s}) = 0 \) m, \( x(2\text{ s}) = 6 \) m, and \( x(4\text{ s}) = 2 \) m, with the particle moving directly between each pair of recorded positions. What is the total distance travelled between \( t = 0 \) s and \( t = 4 \) s?
questions.explanation:
From \( 0 \) s to \( 2 \) s the particle covers \( |6 - 0| = 6 \) m; from \( 2 \) s to \( 4 \) s it covers \( |2 - 6| = 4 \) m (a reversal).

Total distance \( = 6 + 4 = 10 \) m, even though the net displacement is only \( x(4) - x(0) = 2 \) m.
questions.hint: The particle overshoots to \( 6 \) m and then comes back — count that return leg too.
distractor_logic: Confuses distance with displacement, as if the particle never reversed between \( t = 2 \) s and \( t = 4 \) s.
Accounts for only the first leg of motion (\( 0 \) m to \( 6 \) m), ignoring the return leg back to \( 2 \) m.
Adds the two recorded position values \( 6 \) m and \( 2 \) m directly instead of computing the magnitude of each leg's change.

questions.topic: Position, Path Length, and Displacement
questions.question: Two hikers start at the same point on a straight trail and both end up \( 5 \) km east of the start. Hiker A walks directly \( 5 \) km east without stopping. Hiker B walks \( 8 \) km east, then \( 3 \) km west, arriving at the same final point. Compare their displacements and distances.
options: Hiker A has a greater displacement than Hiker B because Hiker A took a shorter path.
Both have the same displacement and the same distance, since they arrive at the same final point.
Hiker B has a smaller distance than Hiker A because the backward leg cancels part of the forward leg.
Both have the same displacement \( (5 \) km east\( ) \), but Hiker B travels a greater distance \( (11 \) km\( ) \) than Hiker A \( (5 \) km\( ) \).
questions.explanation:
Displacement depends only on start and end position, which are identical for both hikers, so both displacements are \( 5 \) km east.

Distance depends on the actual path: Hiker A covers \( 5 \) km, while Hiker B covers \( 8 + 3 = 11 \) km.
questions.hint: Displacement only cares about start and end points; distance cares about every step of the path.
distractor_logic: Assumes displacement depends on which path was taken, when it depends only on the identical start and end positions.
Wrongly assumes distance, like displacement, depends only on the start and end points rather than the actual path taken.
Confuses distance with displacement — reversing direction can reduce net displacement, but every metre walked still adds to the total distance.

questions.topic: Position, Path Length, and Displacement
questions.question: A robot on a straight track executes the following moves in order (positive meaning rightward): \( +5 \) m, \( +3 \) m, \( -9 \) m, \( +2 \) m. What are the total distance travelled and the net displacement?
options: Distance \( = 19 \) m, displacement \( = 1 \) m to the right
Distance \( = 1 \) m, displacement \( = 19 \) m to the right
Distance \( = 19 \) m, displacement \( = 19 \) m to the right
Distance \( = 9 \) m, displacement \( = 1 \) m to the right
questions.explanation:
Distance sums the magnitudes of all four moves: \( 5 + 3 + 9 + 2 = 19 \) m.

Displacement sums the signed moves: \( 5 + 3 - 9 + 2 = 1 \) m to the right.
questions.hint: Keep the negative sign on the third move when summing for displacement, but drop all signs when summing for distance.
distractor_logic: Swaps the distance and displacement values with each other.
Adds all four moves as unsigned magnitudes for displacement too, ignoring the negative sign on the third move.
Uses only the magnitude of the single largest move as the total distance instead of summing all four legs.

questions.topic: Position, Path Length, and Displacement
questions.question: A cyclist starts from home and rides \( 12 \) km to a market. On the way back, after covering \( 7 \) km, she stops at a friend's house that lies directly between the market and home. What is her displacement from home at this point, and what total distance has she covered?
options: Displacement \( = 5 \) km from home (towards the market), distance \( = 19 \) km
questions.explanation:
Displacement from home \( = 12 - 7 = 5 \) km, still on the market side of home.

Distance travelled \( = 12 + 7 = 19 \) km, since both the outward and return legs are actually ridden.
questions.hint: The return leg adds to distance either way, but it subtracts from the net displacement.
distractor_logic: Swaps the distance and displacement values with each other.
Ignores the return leg entirely when computing displacement, as if she never started back from the market.
Forgets to add the return leg to the total distance, counting only the outward trip to the market.

questions.topic: Position, Path Length, and Displacement
questions.question: For a particular journey along a straight road, the magnitude of the displacement is found to be exactly equal to the total distance travelled. What can be concluded about the motion?
options: The object must have returned exactly to its starting point.
The object must have moved at constant speed throughout.
The object moved continuously in one direction without ever reversing.
The object must have covered zero distance.
questions.explanation:
Distance exceeds the magnitude of displacement whenever the object reverses direction at any point.

The two quantities are equal only when there is no reversal at all, i.e. the motion is entirely in one direction.
questions.hint: Think about what kind of reversal would make distance grow while displacement shrinks — then rule that out.
distractor_logic: Describes the opposite situation — returning to the start would make the displacement zero, not equal to the distance.
Introduces speed, which is unrelated: the equality depends on the direction of motion, not on how fast the object travelled.
Confuses the equality condition with the unrelated special case where no motion happens at all.

questions.topic: Position, Path Length, and Displacement
questions.question: A particle moves \( 3 \) m east, then \( 4 \) m east, then \( 2 \) m west. A student calculates the displacement by adding the magnitudes of all three legs as \( 3 + 4 + 2 = 9 \) m. What is wrong with this calculation, and what is the correct displacement?
options: The student's calculation is correct; the displacement is indeed \( 9 \) m east.
The student should have subtracted all three legs instead of adding them; the correct displacement is \( -3 \) m.
The \( 9 \) m value is actually the correct distance travelled, but the displacement equals half of that, i.e. \( 4.5 \) m east.
The student ignored the reversal in direction on the last leg; the correct displacement is \( 5 \) m east.
questions.explanation:
Displacement must treat the westward leg as negative: \( 3 + 4 - 2 = 5 \) m east.

The student's \( 9 \) m is actually the total distance travelled, not the displacement.
questions.hint: Assign a sign to each leg based on its direction before adding — don't just add lengths.
distractor_logic: Accepts the flawed calculation, which is really the total distance travelled (legs added as unsigned magnitudes), not the displacement.
Proposes subtracting every leg instead of correctly assigning the sign of each individual leg based on its own direction.
Invents an unrelated halving rule instead of correctly applying the sign convention to each leg before summing.

questions.topic: Velocity: Average, Instantaneous, and Relative Velocity
questions.question: A car travels the first half of a journey at \( 40 \) km/h and the second half (equal distance) at \( 60 \) km/h. What is the average speed for the entire journey?
questions.explanation:
Let each half have distance \( d \). Time for first half \( = \dfrac{d}{40} \), time for second half \( = \dfrac{d}{60} \).

Total time \( = \dfrac{d}{40}+\dfrac{d}{60} = \dfrac{d}{24} \). Average speed \( = \dfrac{2d}{d/24} = 48 \) km/h.
questions.hint: Because the two legs cover equal distances (not equal times), you cannot simply average the two speeds.
distractor_logic: Computes average speed as the simple numerical average of the two speeds \( \frac{40+60}{2} \), which is only valid when equal time (not equal distance) is spent at each speed.
Uses only the first leg's speed, ignoring the second leg of the journey entirely.
Adds the two speeds directly instead of correctly combining them using total distance over total time.

questions.topic: Velocity: Average, Instantaneous, and Relative Velocity
questions.question: A train travels at \( 60 \) km/h for the first \( 3 \) hours and at \( 90 \) km/h for the next \( 3 \) hours of its journey. What is its average speed for the whole journey?
questions.explanation:
Distance in first leg \( = 60\times3=180 \) km; distance in second leg \( = 90\times3=270 \) km.

Average speed \( = \dfrac{180+270}{3+3} = \dfrac{450}{6} = 75 \) km/h. Since the two legs take equal time, this also equals the simple average \( \dfrac{60+90}{2} \).
questions.hint: Here the two legs take equal TIME, not equal distance — check whether the simple average applies in this case.
distractor_logic: Uses only the first leg's speed, ignoring the second leg of the journey entirely.
Uses only the second leg's speed, ignoring the first leg of the journey entirely.
Applies the equal-distance averaging formula \( \frac{2v_1v_2}{v_1+v_2} \), which is only valid when equal distances (not equal times) are covered at each speed.

questions.topic: Velocity: Average, Instantaneous, and Relative Velocity
questions.question: The position of a particle moving along a straight line is given by \( x(t) = 3t^2 - 2t + 1 \), where \( x \) is in metres and \( t \) is in seconds. What is the instantaneous velocity of the particle at \( t = 2 \) s?
questions.explanation:
Instantaneous velocity is \( v(t) = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 6t - 2 \).

At \( t=2 \) s: \( v(2) = 6(2)-2 = 10 \) m/s.
questions.hint: Differentiate \( x(t) \) with respect to \( t \) first, then substitute \( t=2 \) s.
distractor_logic: Evaluates the position function \( x(2) \) itself, mistaking the particle's position for its velocity.
Reads off the coefficient of \( t \) in the derivative without actually substituting \( t=2 \) into the full expression.
Differentiates correctly to get \( v(t) = 6t - 2 \) but forgets to subtract the constant term, computing only \( 6t \) at \( t=2 \).

questions.topic: Velocity: Average, Instantaneous, and Relative Velocity
questions.question: A particle's position is given by \( x(t) = t^2 + 4t \) (metres, \( t \) in seconds). What is its average velocity between \( t = 1 \) s and \( t = 3 \) s?
questions.hint: Average velocity uses the net change in position over the whole interval, divided by the time elapsed — not the derivative at a single instant.
distractor_logic: Computes the displacement \( x(3)-x(1) \) correctly but forgets to divide by the time interval.
Computes the instantaneous velocity at the final instant \( t=3 \) s using the derivative, instead of the average velocity over the whole interval.
Computes the instantaneous velocity at the initial instant \( t=1 \) s using the derivative, instead of the average velocity over the whole interval.

questions.topic: Velocity: Average, Instantaneous, and Relative Velocity
questions.question: Two towns A and B are \( 300 \) km apart on a straight highway. A bus leaves town A towards B at \( 50 \) km/h, and at the same time another bus leaves town B towards A at \( 70 \) km/h. Using the concept of relative velocity, after how much time will the two buses meet?
questions.explanation:
Since the buses move toward each other, their closing speed is the sum of their speeds: \( 50+70=120 \) km/h.

Time to meet \( = \dfrac{300}{120} = 2.5 \) hours.
questions.hint: For two objects approaching each other, add their speeds to get the rate at which the gap between them closes.
distractor_logic: Subtracts the two speeds \( (70-50=20 \) km/h\( ) \) as the closing speed instead of adding them, which is only correct for objects moving in the same direction.
Uses only bus A's speed, ignoring bus B's contribution to the closing speed.
Uses the average of the two speeds \( \left(\dfrac{50+70}{2}=60 \) km/h\( \right) \) as the closing speed instead of their sum.

questions.topic: Velocity: Average, Instantaneous, and Relative Velocity
questions.question: Cyclist Y is \( 8 \) km ahead of Cyclist X on a straight road. Both start moving in the same direction at the same time — X at \( 24 \) km/h and Y at \( 16 \) km/h. Using relative velocity, how long will it take X to catch up with Y?
questions.explanation:
Since both move in the same direction, X's velocity relative to Y is \( 24-16=8 \) km/h.

Time to close the \( 8 \) km gap \( = \dfrac{8}{8} = 1 \) hour.
questions.hint: For two objects moving the same way, subtract their speeds to get the closing speed of the faster one on the slower one.
distractor_logic: Adds the two speeds \( (24+16=40 \) km/h\( ) \) as the closing speed instead of subtracting them, which would only apply if the cyclists moved toward each other.
Uses only Y's speed as the closing speed, ignoring X's own speed entirely.
Inverts the division, computing speed divided by the gap instead of the gap divided by the relative speed.

questions.topic: Velocity: Average, Instantaneous, and Relative Velocity
questions.question: A particle's position is given by \( x(t) = 12t - 3t^2 \) (metres, \( t \) in seconds). At what time is the particle's instantaneous velocity zero?
questions.hint: Differentiate first to get \( v(t) \), then solve \( v(t)=0 \) — not \( x(t)=0 \).
distractor_logic: Sets the position function \( x(t) \) itself equal to zero and solves, instead of setting the velocity function \( v(t) \) equal to zero.
Differentiates correctly to \( v(t)=12-6t \) but divides \( 12 \) by \( 1 \) instead of by \( 6 \) when solving for \( t \).
Mistakes the magnitude of the acceleration (\( 6 \) m/s\(^2\)) for the time at which the velocity is zero.

questions.topic: Velocity: Average, Instantaneous, and Relative Velocity
questions.question: A cheetah runs at \( 90 \) km/h chasing a gazelle that runs at \( 72 \) km/h, both moving in the same direction along a straight path, with the gazelle initially \( 500 \) m ahead. Using relative velocity, how long does it take the cheetah to catch the gazelle?
questions.explanation:
Relative velocity \( = 90-72=18 \) km/h \( = 18\times\tfrac{5}{18} = 5 \) m/s.

Time to close the \( 500 \) m gap \( = \dfrac{500}{5} = 100 \) s.
questions.hint: Convert the relative velocity to m/s (using \( 1 \) km/h \( = \tfrac{5}{18} \) m/s) before dividing into the gap in metres.
distractor_logic: Uses the cheetah's own speed (converted to \( 25 \) m/s) as the closing speed instead of the relative velocity between the two animals.
Uses the gazelle's own speed (converted to \( 20 \) m/s) as the closing speed instead of the relative velocity between the two animals.
Divides the gap by the relative speed still expressed in km/h (\( 18 \)) without converting it to m/s first, mixing units.

questions.topic: Acceleration: Average and Instantaneous
questions.question: The velocity of a particle moving along a straight line is given by \( v(t) = 4t^2 - 3t + 2 \) (m/s, \( t \) in seconds). What is its instantaneous acceleration at \( t = 3 \) s?
questions.hint: Differentiate \( v(t) \) with respect to \( t \) first, then substitute \( t=3 \).
distractor_logic: Evaluates the velocity function \( v(3) \), mistaking the particle's velocity for its acceleration.
Differentiates correctly to \( a(t)=8t-3 \) but forgets to subtract the constant term, computing only \( 8t \) at \( t=3 \).
Reads off the coefficient of \( t \) in the derivative without substituting \( t=3 \) into the full expression.

questions.topic: Acceleration: Average and Instantaneous
questions.question: The position of a particle is given by \( x(t) = 2t^3 - 5t^2 + 4 \) (metres, \( t \) in seconds). What is the particle's instantaneous acceleration at \( t = 2 \) s?
questions.hint: You must differentiate \( x(t) \) twice to reach acceleration — once for velocity, once more for acceleration.
distractor_logic: Differentiates twice correctly in form but forgets to subtract the constant term, computing only \( 12t \) at \( t=2 \).
Differentiates \( x(t) \) only once to get the velocity function, and mistakes the resulting velocity at \( t=2 \) for the acceleration.
Reads off the coefficient of \( t \) in \( a(t)=12t-10 \) without substituting \( t=2 \) into the full expression.

questions.topic: Acceleration: Average and Instantaneous
questions.question: A cyclist accelerates from \( 2 \) m/s to \( 6 \) m/s in the first \( 4 \) s, and then from \( 6 \) m/s to \( 14 \) m/s in the next \( 2 \) s. What is the average acceleration over the entire \( 6 \) s interval?
questions.explanation:
Total change in velocity \( = 14-2 = 12 \) m/s over the total time \( 4+2=6 \) s.

Average acceleration \( = \dfrac{12}{6} = 2 \) m/s\(^2\).
questions.hint: Use the overall change in velocity divided by the overall time — not the individual segment accelerations.
distractor_logic: Averages the two segment accelerations \( \left(\dfrac{1+4}{2}\right) \) instead of finding the overall change in velocity divided by the overall time.
Uses only the second segment's acceleration, ignoring the first segment entirely.
Computes the correct total change in velocity but divides by only the first segment's time instead of the full \( 6 \) s.

questions.topic: Acceleration: Average and Instantaneous
questions.question: A ball is thrown vertically upward (\( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\)) and, taking the upward direction as positive, its velocity decreases from \( 20 \) m/s to \( 0 \) m/s in \( 2 \) s due to gravity. What is its average acceleration during this interval, and how does it compare to \( g \)?
options: \( 10 \) m/s\(^2\), positive, since gravity always acts downward and downward is being treated as positive here
\( -20 \) m/s\(^2\), since the full velocity change of \( 20 \) m/s should be reported directly as the acceleration
\( 0 \) m/s\(^2\), since the ball momentarily comes to rest at the top
\( -10 \) m/s\(^2\), equal in magnitude to \( g \) but negative since upward was taken as positive
questions.explanation:
Average acceleration \( = \dfrac{0-20}{2} = -10 \) m/s\(^2\).

This has magnitude \( g=10 \) m/s\(^2\) but is negative, because gravity acts downward while the chosen positive direction is upward.
questions.hint: The stated sign convention (upward positive) fixes the sign of \( g \) throughout — gravity itself never changes direction.
distractor_logic: Wrongly assumes the sign of \( g \) depends on which way gravity physically acts rather than on the sign convention chosen for the problem (upward positive).
Reports the full change in velocity directly as the acceleration, forgetting to divide by the time interval.
Confuses the ball's momentarily zero velocity at the highest point with the acceleration also being zero there, when gravity continues to act throughout.

questions.topic: Acceleration: Average and Instantaneous
questions.question: A particle's velocity is given by \( v(t) = 6 - 3t \) (m/s, \( t \) in seconds). At \( t = 2 \) s, the particle's velocity is momentarily zero. What is its acceleration at this instant?
questions.explanation: \( a(t) = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = -3 \) m/s\(^2\), a constant. This value does not depend on \( t \), so the acceleration at \( t=2 \) s is still \( -3 \) m/s\(^2\), even though the velocity is momentarily zero there.
questions.hint: A momentarily zero velocity does not mean the acceleration is also zero — differentiate \( v(t) \) to check.
distractor_logic: Assumes that because the velocity is momentarily zero, the acceleration must also be zero at that instant.
Evaluates the constant term of \( v(t) \) instead of differentiating to find the acceleration.
Gets the correct magnitude but drops the negative sign of the constant deceleration.

questions.topic: Acceleration: Average and Instantaneous
questions.question: A particle's velocity changes from \( 8 \) m/s to \( -4 \) m/s over an interval of \( 3 \) s while moving along a straight line. What is its average acceleration?
questions.explanation: Average acceleration \( = \dfrac{-4-8}{3} = \dfrac{-12}{3} = -4 \) m/s\(^2\).
questions.hint: Carefully subtract the signed initial velocity from the signed final velocity, including the negative sign, before dividing.
distractor_logic: Gets the correct magnitude but drops the negative sign.
Adds the two signed velocities \( (8+(-4)) \) instead of subtracting them to find the change in velocity.
Computes the change in velocity correctly but forgets to divide by the time interval.

questions.topic: Acceleration: Average and Instantaneous
questions.question: A particle's velocity is recorded as \( v(2\text{ s}) = 14 \) m/s and \( v(6\text{ s}) = 26 \) m/s. What is its average acceleration over this interval?
questions.explanation: Average acceleration \( = \dfrac{v(6)-v(2)}{6-2} = \dfrac{26-14}{4} = 3 \) m/s\(^2\).
questions.hint: Divide the change in velocity by the actual time interval between the two recorded instants, not by either time value alone.
distractor_logic: Divides the change in velocity by the initial time value alone \( (12/2=6) \) instead of the interval \( \Delta t \).
Divides the change in velocity by the final time value alone \( (12/6=2) \) instead of the interval \( \Delta t \).
Forgets to divide by the time interval altogether, reporting only the change in velocity.

questions.topic: Acceleration: Average and Instantaneous
questions.question: A particle is moving in the negative \( x \)-direction and has a negative acceleration. What does this tell us about its speed?
options: The particle's speed is decreasing, since its acceleration is negative.
The particle must be moving in the positive direction now.
The particle's speed remains constant, since acceleration only affects direction, not speed.
The particle's speed is increasing, since its velocity and acceleration have the same sign.
questions.explanation: Speed increases when velocity and acceleration have the same sign, and decreases when they have opposite signs. Here both are negative, so the particle is speeding up as it moves in the negative direction.
questions.hint: Don't judge speeding up or slowing down from the sign of acceleration alone — compare it to the sign of the velocity.
distractor_logic: Wrongly assumes negative acceleration always means slowing down, without checking whether it has the same or opposite sign as the velocity.
Confuses the sign of the acceleration with an immediate reversal of the velocity's own sign.
Fundamentally misunderstands acceleration as affecting only direction, when it also governs the rate of change of speed.

questions.topic: Kinematic Equations for Uniformly Accelerated Motion
questions.question: A ball is thrown vertically upward with an initial velocity of \( 20 \) m/s. Taking upward as positive and using \( g = 10 \) m/s\(^2\), how long does it take to reach its maximum height?
questions.explanation: At maximum height, \( v=0 \). Using \( v=u+at \) with \( a=-g=-10 \) m/s\(^2\): \( 0=20+(-10)t \), so \( t=2 \) s.
questions.hint: Since upward is positive here, gravity's acceleration must be entered as \( -10 \) m/s\(^2\), not \( +10 \).
distractor_logic: Keeps the acceleration positive (\( a=+10 \) m/s\(^2\)) instead of assigning it a negative sign, since upward was chosen as positive and gravity acts downward.
Mistakenly halves the given value of \( g \) instead of using the full \( 10 \) m/s\(^2\) stated in the problem.
Inverts the ratio, computing acceleration divided by initial velocity instead of the other way round.

questions.topic: Kinematic Equations for Uniformly Accelerated Motion
questions.question: A stone is thrown vertically upward with an initial velocity of \( 30 \) m/s. Taking upward as positive and using \( g = 10 \) m/s\(^2\), what maximum height does it reach above the point of projection?
questions.hint: Keep \( a \) negative throughout, since gravity opposes the chosen upward-positive direction.
distractor_logic: Uses the acceleration as positive (\( a=+10 \)) instead of negative, yielding a nonsensical negative result for a height.
Forgets the factor of \( 2 \) in \( 2as \), computing \( s=u^2/a=900/10=90 \) m instead.
Forgets to account for \( 2a \) altogether, reporting \( u^2 \) directly as the height.

questions.topic: Kinematic Equations for Uniformly Accelerated Motion
questions.question: A ball is dropped from a height and falls freely under gravity, starting from rest. Taking downward as positive and using \( g = 9.8 \) m/s\(^2\), what is its velocity after falling for \( 3 \) s?
questions.explanation: Using \( v=u+at \) with \( u=0 \) and \( a=+9.8 \) m/s\(^2\) (downward is positive here): \( v=0+(9.8)(3)=29.4 \) m/s, downward.
questions.hint: Here downward is the chosen positive direction, so \( g \) itself is entered as positive.
distractor_logic: Wrongly keeps \( g \) negative even though downward was chosen as the positive direction in this problem.
Gets the correct magnitude but assigns the wrong direction, forgetting that downward is positive here.
Inverts the ratio, dividing \( g \) by \( t \) instead of multiplying them.

questions.topic: Kinematic Equations for Uniformly Accelerated Motion
questions.question: A ball is thrown vertically upward with an initial velocity of \( 15 \) m/s. Taking upward as positive and using \( g = 10 \) m/s\(^2\), what is its velocity at \( t = 2 \) s?
options: \( 5 \) m/s, upward — the ball is still rising
questions.explanation: Using \( v=u+at \) with \( a=-10 \) m/s\(^2\): \( v=15+(-10)(2)=15-20=-5 \) m/s — i.e. \( 5 \) m/s downward, since the ball has already passed its peak and is falling back.
questions.hint: A negative result here is physical, not an error — it means the ball has already turned around.
distractor_logic: Gets the correct magnitude but wrongly assumes the ball must still be moving upward simply because it hasn't yet returned to the ground.
Keeps the acceleration positive throughout instead of negative, since upward was chosen as positive and gravity should oppose it.
Uses only the acceleration term \( at \), forgetting to add the initial velocity \( u \).

questions.topic: Kinematic Equations for Uniformly Accelerated Motion
questions.question: A ball is thrown vertically upward from the ground with an initial velocity of \( 20 \) m/s. Taking upward as positive and using \( g = 10 \) m/s\(^2\), what is its displacement from the ground at \( t = 3 \) s?
questions.explanation: Using \( s=ut+\tfrac12at^2 \) with \( a=-10 \) m/s\(^2\): \( s=(20)(3)+\tfrac12(-10)(3)^2 = 60-45=15 \) m above the ground.
questions.hint: Substitute the negative sign of \( a \) into the \( \tfrac12at^2 \) term, not just the \( v=u+at \) equation.
distractor_logic: Keeps \( a \) positive (\( +10 \)) instead of negative, computing \( 60+45=105 \) m.
Computes only the \( ut \) term, forgetting the \( \tfrac12at^2 \) contribution.
Computes the magnitude correctly using the right sign of \( a \), but then attaches an extra, unwarranted negative sign to the final displacement itself.

questions.topic: Kinematic Equations for Uniformly Accelerated Motion
questions.question: A car moving at \( 20 \) m/s applies its brakes and decelerates uniformly at \( 5 \) m/s\(^2\). Taking the car's direction of motion as positive, what distance does it travel before coming to rest?
questions.explanation: Using \( v^2=u^2+2as \) with \( a=-5 \) m/s\(^2\) (braking opposes the direction of motion) and \( v=0 \): \( 0=400+2(-5)s \), so \( 10s=400 \) and \( s=40 \) m.
questions.hint: Braking always opposes the direction of motion, so \( a \) must be negative here, even though no direction was reversed.
distractor_logic: Keeps the acceleration positive (\( +5 \) m/s\(^2\)) instead of negative, ignoring that braking opposes the chosen positive direction of motion.
